title: GPTs are GPTs: An Early Look at the Labor Market Impact Potential of Large Language Models
extended_summary:
This paper asks how much of the U.S. labor market could be affected by large language models (LLMs) such as GPTs, and whether these models resemble general-purpose technologies. Rather than studying education or student learning outcomes, the paper builds a task-based exposure rubric to estimate whether LLMs, or LLM-powered software built on top of them, could reduce the time needed to complete specific occupational tasks while maintaining quality.

The authors apply this rubric to O*NET occupation and task data, combining human annotations with GPT-4 classifications. The empirical context is the U.S. workforce across 1,016 occupations, using 19,265 tasks and 2,087 detailed work activities. They compare exposure patterns across wages, job zones, education levels, and skill requirements, and benchmark their measures against prior occupational exposure studies.

The main conclusion is that LLMs have broad task exposure potential: roughly 15% of tasks may be directly accelerated by LLMs alone, and the share rises substantially when complementary software is included. The paper finds that exposure is widespread across occupations, somewhat higher in higher-wage and more highly educated jobs, and positively related to programming and writing skills but negatively related to science and critical thinking skills. No directly empirical ChatGPT mathematics intervention study in grades 6–8 is present; the closest evidence is this occupation-level task exposure analysis, which includes mathematics as a skill correlate rather than an educational intervention.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a grey-literature working paper about labor-market exposure of occupations to LLMs, not an empirical K-12 education intervention study. It does not evaluate any classroom, tutoring, or student outcome with a counterfactual design.
impact_tier_rationale: There is no direct educational impact estimate for grades 6–8 mathematics or any student outcome. The paper only provides occupational exposure/risk estimates and comparator evidence from prior AI-exposure studies, so it does not support an intervention impact claim for the requested search.
